concept: Q is n×d_k queries, K is m×d_k keys, V is m×d_v values. QK^T scores every query against every key. Dividing by √d_k holds the variance of that dot product near 1: summing d_k unit-variance products gives variance d_k, so without the scale the logits spread as √d_k, the softmax saturates toward one-hot, and its Jacobian vanishes. Softmax over the key axis turns scores into a distribution, and multiplying by V takes the weighted average. Causal masking adds −∞ to positions j>i before the softmax so future tokens get exactly zero weight.
example: GPT-2 small: d_model=768, 12 heads, d_k=64, n=1024. Per head QK^T is 1024×1024 = 1.05M scores; across 12 heads that is 12.6M scores and about 4.2 GFLOPs for the two matmuls per layer. Unscaled, a dot product of unit-variance entries over 64 terms has std √64 = 8, so logits span roughly ±24 and softmax puts over 0.99 on a single key. Dividing by 8 pulls the std back to 1.
interview_question: A colleague drops the 1/√d_k term and reports that training stalls almost immediately at d_k=64 but is perfectly fine at d_k=8. Derive why, and say what you would expect to see in the attention gradients.
answer_points: q·k sums d_k products; with unit-variance independent entries Var = d_k, so logit std is √d_k — 8 at d_k=64 versus 2.8 at d_k=8
Wide logits drive softmax toward one-hot, and its Jacobian diag(s) − ss^T → 0 there, so no gradient reaches W_Q or W_K
d_k=8 still lands inside the softmax's responsive band, which is why the small case trains normally
The scale is a constant and could in principle be folded into W_Q at init — it is not, because the weights drift during training while √d_k stays exact

concept: W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O are each d_model×d_model, so attention costs 4d² per layer no matter how many heads there are — splitting into h heads only reshapes d_model into h·d_h. A 4×-expansion FFN adds two d×4d matrices, or 8d², making the block 12d² and putting attention at one third of it. Multiply by L for the body. Embedding and unembedding are V·d_model and sit outside this count.
example: GPT-3 175B: d_model=12288, L=96. Attention is 4·12288² = 604M per layer × 96 = 58B. FFN is 8·12288² = 1.21B per layer × 96 = 116B. Body total 174B, plus a 50257×12288 embedding at 0.6B — that is the 175B. Do the same for GPT-2 small (d=768, L=12): 12·768²·12 = 85M body, but the 50257×768 embedding adds 39M, a third again.
interview_question: You are asked at a whiteboard to size a 96-layer, d_model=12288 decoder in under a minute, then to say what fraction of it a LoRA placed only on the attention projections would touch. Work it through.
answer_points: 12d² per layer: 4d² attention plus 8d² FFN at 4× expansion, so 12·12288²·96 ≈ 174B
Head count never enters — h heads of width d_model/h partition the same four matrices
Embedding plus unembedding is V·d_model: negligible at 175B, but a third of a 125M model
Attention is exactly one third of the body, so attention-only LoRA can reach at most 33% of it — which is why modern recipes also target the FFN projections
GQA breaks the 4d² rule: W_K and W_V shrink to d_model·(G·d_h), putting LLaMA-2 70B attention nearer 2.25d²

formula: \text{bytes} = 2 \cdot L \cdot S \cdot G \cdot d_h \cdot b_{\text{dtype}} \cdot B
concept: Every layer stores one K and one V tensor per KV head, which is the leading 2. L is layers, S positions in context, G key/value heads (under GQA fewer than the query heads H), d_h the per-head width, b_dtype bytes per element, B concurrent sequences. It is linear in both S and B and is never amortised: weights are paid once for the whole fleet, cache is paid per request per token.
example: LLaMA-2 70B: L=80, G=8, d_h=128, fp16. At S=4096, B=1 that is 2·80·4096·8·128·2 = 10.5 GB. Weights are 140 GB, so on a 2×80 GB A100 node only 20 GB remains — under two concurrent 4k requests before OOM. Switch the cache to FP8 and it halves to 5.2 GB, buying four. Without GQA (G=H=64) the same request would need 84 GB and would not fit at all.
interview_question: Your fleet holds 40 concurrent requests at 512-token contexts but only 4 once average context reaches 4k, and GPU utilisation falls with it. Derive the memory numbers and rank the fixes you would ship.
answer_points: Cache is linear in S·B, so 8× the context is 8× the bytes and the batch that fits shrinks 8×
Small batch means decode still reads all 140 GB of weights to emit few tokens — arithmetic intensity collapses and the GPU idles on HBM
GQA already bought 8× here (64 query heads, 8 KV heads); remaining levers are FP8/INT8 cache, PagedAttention against fragmentation, and prefix caching for shared system prompts
Utilisation falling is the tell that this is a memory-capacity problem showing up as a bandwidth problem, not a compute shortage
MLA, as in DeepSeek-V2, compresses KV into a single per-token latent — roughly a tenth of GQA, and an axis independent of quantisation

concept: H is the number of query heads, G the number of key/value groups. Query heads are untouched; each group of H/G query heads shares one K and one V projection, so the cache shrinks by exactly H/G. The saving is in the KV projections and the cache only — attention FLOPs barely move, because K and V are broadcast back across their group before the matmul. G=H recovers plain MHA, G=1 is multi-query attention.
example: LLaMA-2 70B: d_model=8192, H=64, d_h=128, L=80, G=8. Cache falls 8×, from 84 GB to 10.5 GB at S=4096 fp16. W_K and W_V each shrink from 8192×8192 to 8192×1024, saving 117M params per layer and 9.4B across 80 layers. The checkpoint is produced by mean-pooling each group's K and V projections from an MHA model and uptraining on a small fraction of the original token budget, not by pretraining from scratch.
interview_question: You have an MHA checkpoint that will not serve at your target concurrency. Compute what G you need to fit a batch of 16 at 4k context in 40 GB, and explain how you would obtain that checkpoint without pretraining again.
answer_points: Cache scales linearly in G: solve 2·L·S·G·d_h·b·B ≤ 40 GB for G and round down to a power of two
Query heads stay at H, so attention FLOPs are essentially unchanged — this buys memory bandwidth and capacity, not compute
Convert by mean-pooling each group's K and V projection weights, then uptrain briefly on in-distribution data
G=1 (MQA) saves the most but costs quality and destabilises training; G≈8 is the usual knee
G must stay at or above the tensor-parallel degree, or KV heads have to be replicated across ranks and the memory saving partly evaporates

concept: Split each head's query and key into d/2 two-dimensional pairs and rotate pair j at position m by angle m·θ_j, with θ_j = base^(−2j/d). Because rotations are orthogonal, the dot product of a rotated query and a rotated key depends only on the offset m−n: absolute positions go in, a relative score comes out. Nothing is added to the residual stream — RoPE touches Q and K only, inside every layer, and never V.
example: LLaMA-2 has d_h=128, so 64 frequency pairs, base=10000. Wavelengths run from 2π ≈ 6.3 tokens at j=0 to about 54000 tokens at j=63. At S=4096 only roughly the first 45 of 64 pairs ever complete a full rotation during training; the rest act as slowly varying absolute features. LLaMA-3 raises base to 500000, stretching the longest wavelength to about 2.5M tokens, which is what supports its 128k context.
interview_question: Show that a rotary-embedded attention score depends only on m−n, then explain why feeding such a model sequences 8× longer than it trained on degrades sharply while position interpolation does not.
answer_points: Rotations are orthogonal: ⟨R_m q, R_n k⟩ = q^T R_m^T R_n k = q^T R_{n−m} k, so only the offset survives
High-frequency pairs wrap many times during training and stay in distribution; low-frequency pairs at large m reach angles never seen, and those out-of-distribution rotations wreck the score
Position interpolation rescales m by L_train/L_test so every angle stays inside the trained range, paying for it in high-frequency resolution
RoPE is re-applied per layer to Q and K only, never to V or the residual stream, so it does not accumulate with depth the way a learned absolute embedding does

concept: NTK-aware scaling extends context by changing the RoPE base rather than the positions. Raising the base stretches low-frequency pairs by roughly the full factor s — exactly where out-of-distribution angles appear — while leaving high-frequency pairs almost untouched, so local token-order resolution survives. The d/(d−2) exponent is chosen so the lowest-frequency pair lands at precisely s after scaling. Position interpolation instead divides every position by s and blurs all frequencies equally.
example: LLaMA-2, d_h=128, base=10000, extending 4096 → 32768 gives s=8 and base_new = 10000·8^(128/126) ≈ 8.3×10⁴. The lowest-frequency pair's wavelength moves from about 54000 to about 4.3×10⁵ tokens, comfortably past 32768, while the j=0 pair moves only from 6.28 to 6.29 tokens. Plain interpolation at s=8 would instead have stretched that j=0 wavelength to 50 tokens — an 8× loss of local resolution.
interview_question: You must take a 4k-trained RoPE model to 32k with only a few hundred fine-tuning steps. Compare NTK base scaling against position interpolation numerically at both ends of the frequency spectrum, and say which you ship.
answer_points: PI divides all positions by s, so every wavelength stretches 8× including j=0, costing local order resolution uniformly
NTK scales the base, making the effect frequency-dependent: lowest pair stretched ≈s, highest pair essentially unchanged
The d/(d−2) exponent exists so the j = d/2−1 pair lands at exactly s — it is not a fudge factor
NTK degrades if pushed zero-shot well past its target s; YaRN combines ramped per-band interpolation with an attention temperature term and needs far fewer tokens than PI to recover

concept: No positional embedding at all. A fixed, non-learned linear penalty is subtracted from each attention logit in proportion to the distance between query i and key j. Head h gets its own slope m_h from a geometric sequence, so with n heads the slopes span 2^(−8/n) down to 2^−8. Small-slope heads see almost globally, large-slope heads behave as local windows. Nothing is added to Q, K, or the residual stream, so the penalty extends to any length for free.
example: With n=16 heads the slopes run from 2^(−0.5) = 0.71 down to 2^−8 = 0.0039. At a distance of 1000 tokens the sharpest head subtracts 710 from its logit — a hard zero after softmax — while the flattest subtracts 3.9, about one e-fold of down-weighting. That spread across heads is why a 1024-trained ALiBi model still holds perplexity past 2048, where learned absolute embeddings have no values to use at all.
interview_question: Your model must serve documents up to 3× the training length with no fine-tuning budget. Argue for or against ALiBi over RoPE, and explain what the per-head slope schedule actually buys you.
answer_points: The bias is fixed and content-independent, added to logits pre-softmax, so there are no positional parameters that can go out of distribution
Geometric slopes give a head-wise mixture of receptive fields — multi-scale local and global attention for free
The extrapolation is real but comes from recency bias, so it helps perplexity more than genuine long-range retrieval; test on needle-in-a-haystack, not just perplexity
The bias matrix is dense and length-dependent, so it fights fused kernels: FlashAttention needs an ALiBi-aware variant, whereas RoPE is applied to Q and K before the kernel and costs it nothing

concept: Statistics are taken across the feature dimension of a single token, never across the batch — that is what makes it independent of batch size and sequence length, and what lets it behave identically at batch 1 during decoding. γ and β restore the ability to express a non-zero-mean, non-unit-variance activation. ε sits inside the square root and is typically 1e-5; placing it outside is a classic bug that surfaces in fp16 when σ² is small.
example: GPT-3 d_model=12288: 2·12288 = 24576 params per LayerNorm, 2 per block, 96 blocks — 4.7M params, 0.003% of 175B. The backward pass, though, needs dL/dy, x̂ and two reductions over d, touching roughly 4× the activation tensor. At batch 8 × 2048 tokens × 12288 in fp16 one activation tensor is 402 MB, so a single LayerNorm moves about 1.6 GB of HBM per step. That gap is why fusing it matters far more than its parameter count suggests.
interview_question: Derive dL/dx for LayerNorm, then explain why the naive autograd version is memory-bound while a fused kernel is not — and what changes if you move the norm from post- to pre-residual.
answer_points: dL/dx = (γ/σ)·[dL/dy − mean(dL/dy) − x̂·mean(dL/dy·x̂)]; the two mean terms appear because μ and σ each depend on every x_i
That is two reductions over d plus elementwise work — naive autograd materialises every intermediate to HBM, so it is bandwidth-bound and fusion collapses four tensor round-trips into one

Pre-LN puts the norm inside the residual branch, leaving the identity path unnormalised so gradients reach layer 0 unattenuated and warmup becomes optional; Post-LN diverges at depth without careful warmup
ε must be inside the sqrt, and in fp16 the mean and variance reductions must accumulate in fp32 or σ² underflows on near-zero activations

concept: Drops both the mean subtraction and the β shift, leaving only re-scaling. The bet is that LayerNorm's benefit comes from scale invariance rather than re-centring, and empirically that holds. The result is one reduction instead of two dependent ones, one learnable vector instead of two, and no μ to keep for the backward pass — cheaper in traffic and in registers. Every major open model since LLaMA has used it.
example: LLaMA-2 7B: d_model=4096, so 4096 params per norm against LayerNorm's 8192; at 2 per block over 32 blocks that is 262k versus 524k params, negligible either way. The real win is the kernel: Σx² is a single reduction, whereas LayerNorm cannot start σ² until μ is finished — two dependent block-wide syncs per 4096-wide row. Meta kept RMSNorm through LLaMA-3 405B for exactly that reason.
interview_question: RMSNorm removes mean-centring and the bias term, yet quality holds. Explain what invariance the normalisation is actually providing, then describe a regime where dropping the centring would hurt you.
answer_points: The property that matters is invariance to rescaling of the input row; re-centring is not what stabilises training
One reduction instead of two dependent ones, no μ stored for backward, one learnable vector instead of two
With no β, any needed offset must come from the following linear layer — models that also drop biases lean on the residual stream to carry it

If activations carry a large shared DC component, RMS is dominated by that offset and the normalised output loses dynamic range; this is part of why RMSNorm models are sensitive to outlier channels and why schemes like SmoothQuant target exactly those

concept: A gated linear unit: one projection produces values, a second produces a multiplicative gate passed through SiLU, and their elementwise product is projected back down. The gate lets the layer suppress or pass each hidden unit conditionally on the input, which a plain ReLU or GELU MLP cannot do. The cost is three weight matrices instead of two, so the hidden width is cut to 8/3·d_model to keep the parameter count level with a 4× ReLU FFN.
example: LLaMA-2 7B, d_model=4096. A 4× ReLU FFN would be 2·4096·16384 = 134M params per layer. SwiGLU uses hidden = 8/3·4096 = 10923, rounded up to 11008 for alignment, over three matrices: 3·4096·11008 = 135M — the same budget. Across 32 layers that is 4.3B of the model's 6.7B, against 2.15B in attention, so the FFN is where most of a modern 7B actually lives.
interview_question: Given a fixed parameter budget for the FFN block, derive the hidden width that makes SwiGLU parameter-neutral against a 4× ReLU MLP, then justify whether you would spend the budget there at all.
answer_points: Three d×h matrices versus two d×4d matrices: 3dh = 8d² gives h = 8/3·d
In practice h is rounded to a multiple of 256 — 11008 for LLaMA-2 7B — so the GEMM tiles cleanly on tensor cores
The gate is the actual mechanism: a multiplicative interaction, not merely a different nonlinearity

The extra matrix costs a third GEMM and another activation tensor, so SwiGLU is slightly worse for memory-bound decode even at equal parameters; gate and up are usually fused into one 2h-wide GEMM to claw that back

concept: Cross-entropy of the next token, averaged over the N supervised positions. Every position is trained in parallel but each is conditioned only on its causal prefix, which is what makes one forward pass worth N gradient signals. Perplexity exponentiates the loss back into an interpretable unit: the effective number of equally likely tokens the model is choosing among. Using natural log the loss is in nats and PPL = e^L; using log base 2 it is bits per token and PPL = 2^L.
example: Uniform guessing over GPT-2's 50257-token vocabulary gives L = ln 50257 = 10.82 nats, PPL = 50257. A trained GPT-2 medium sits near L = 3.0, PPL ≈ 20. Cutting loss by exactly ln 2 = 0.69 nats halves perplexity, 20 → 10, which is why the last tenths of a nat cost so much compute: the scaling curve is a power law in loss, and perplexity magnifies small loss moves into large-looking ones.
interview_question: Team A reports perplexity 12 and team B reports 9 on the same corpus, and B claims the better model. What do you check before believing it, and how much loss does that 3-point gap actually represent?
answer_points: PPL = e^L, so 12 → 9 is ln(12/9) = 0.29 nats — a small absolute move on the loss curve, not a 25% improvement in anything
Perplexity is per token, so it is meaningless across different tokenisers: a tokeniser that splits more finely earns lower per-token loss for free. Normalise to bits per byte to compare
Check the evaluation stride — sliding-window scoring with full context beats non-overlapping chunks on the identical model
Check test-set contamination, and whether the mean is taken per token or per document; per-document averaging silently over-weights short documents

concept: For a fixed training compute budget C, loss is minimised when parameters N and training tokens D grow in roughly equal proportion — about 20 tokens per parameter. Earlier scaling work scaled N far faster than D and produced undertrained giants. The crucial limitation: this is compute-optimality at training time only. It says nothing about inference, where a smaller model trained well past 20N is cheaper to serve at equal quality.
example: GPT-3: N=175B, D=300B, only 1.7 tokens per parameter against the optimal 20, at 6ND = 3.2×10²³ FLOPs. Chinchilla is 70B on 1.4T tokens, 5.9×10²³ FLOPs, matching Gopher's 280B-on-300B budget of 5.0×10²³ and beating it broadly with 4× fewer parameters. Compute-optimal GPT-3 would have needed 20·175B = 3.5T tokens. LLaMA-3 8B deliberately goes the other way: 15T tokens, 1875 tokens per parameter, 94× past Chinchilla.
interview_question: You have a fixed 10²³ FLOP training budget and the model will serve 10¹² tokens of production traffic. Compute the Chinchilla-optimal size, then argue whether you should actually train that model.
answer_points: C = 6ND with D = 20N gives C = 120N², so N = √(C/120) — at 10²³ that is about 29B parameters on 580B tokens
Chinchilla minimises training loss per training FLOP and ignores inference completely
Inference costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so 10¹² served tokens on a 29B model is 5.8×10²² FLOPs — over half the training budget, paid again and again
So the right move is usually smaller-and-longer than Chinchilla: the loss penalty for overtraining an 8B is small and the curve is near-flat there, while serving cost scales linearly in N forever
The 20× ratio is also data-dependent — it was fitted on a specific corpus, and repeated-epoch data does not count the same as fresh tokens

concept: Each parameter takes part in one multiply and one add per token in the forward pass, giving 2N FLOPs per token. The backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights — two more passes of the same size — giving 4N. Total 6N per token over D tokens. The estimate drops attention's quadratic term, which is safe while S is small against d_model, and treats normalisation and softmax as lower order.
example: LLaMA-2 7B on 2T tokens: 6·7×10⁹·2×10¹² = 8.4×10²² FLOPs. On 1024 A100s at 312 TFLOP/s bf16 and a realistic 40% MFU, effective throughput is 1.28×10¹⁷ FLOP/s, so the run takes 6.6×10⁵ s — about 7.6 days. The neglected attention term scales as S/(6·d_model) = 4096/24576 ≈ 17%, so at 4k context this estimate runs low by roughly that much.
interview_question: A director asks how long a 70B run on 3T tokens will take on your 2048-H100 cluster, and what it will cost. Derive it end to end, then state the assumption most likely to make you wrong.
answer_points: H100 SXM is ~990 TFLOP/s dense bf16; at 2048 GPUs and 40% MFU that is 8.1×10¹⁷ effective FLOP/s → 1.55×10⁶ s ≈ 18 days
The 6 decomposes as 2 forward + 4 backward, because backward produces both activation and weight gradients

MFU is the assumption that kills the estimate — it swings between 25% and 55% with parallelism strategy, sequence length and interconnect, and activation recomputation adds roughly another 1N–2N per token, pushing the constant from 6 toward 8

formula: \begin{gathered} M \approx \underbrace{2P}_{\text{bf16 weights}} + \underbrace{2P}_{\text{bf16 grads}} \\[3pt] +\ \underbrace{4P + 4P + 4P}_{\text{fp32 master},\ m,\ v}\ =\ 16P \text{ bytes} \end{gathered}
concept: Mixed-precision AdamW keeps bf16 weights and gradients for the math, plus an fp32 master copy of the weights and the two fp32 moment estimates used by the update rule. That is 2+2+4+4+4 = 16 bytes per parameter, before a single activation is stored. Activations are a separate budget scaling with batch × sequence × layers, and they are what activation checkpointing trades away for recompute.
example: A 7B model: 16·7×10⁹ = 112 GB of weights, gradients and optimizer state alone — already past one 80 GB H100 before any activations. ZeRO stage 3 shards all three across ranks, so on 8 GPUs it is 14 GB each. Switching to 8-bit Adam moments takes m and v from 4P to 1P each, dropping 16P to 10P, or 70 GB, which then fits on a single card.
interview_question: Your 7B run OOMs on 8×80 GB with a batch size that should comfortably fit. Account for every byte, then order the fixes by what each costs you in throughput.
answer_points: 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision AdamW: 2 bf16 weights + 2 grads + 4 fp32 master + 4 m + 4 v = 112 GB at 7B
Activations are the other half of the budget and scale with batch × seq × L — they are what actually varies run to run
Order by cost: ZeRO-2 then ZeRO-3 (pays in communication, not compute), 8-bit optimizer states (nearly free), activation checkpointing (~30% throughput), gradient accumulation last
The fp32 master copy is not optional — bf16 has 8 mantissa bits, and a typical update is 10⁻⁴ of the weight, so updating bf16 weights directly rounds most updates to zero

formula: \begin{gathered} W' = W_{0} + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA \\[3pt] B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}} \\[3pt] |\theta| = r\,(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) \end{gathered}
concept: Freeze W₀ and learn a rank-r update factored as BA. A starts from a normal distribution and B starts at exactly zero, so BA = 0 at step 0 and training begins precisely at the base checkpoint. The α/r scaling keeps the effective step size roughly independent of r, so sweeping rank does not require re-sweeping the learning rate. At inference BA folds back into W₀, adding zero latency.
example: LLaMA-2 7B with r=16 on all linear layers: q,k,v,o are 4096×4096, giving 4·16·8192 = 524k params; the FFN's gate, up and down involve 4096 and 11008, giving 3·16·15104 = 725k. That is 1.25M per layer, 40M across 32 layers — 0.6% of 6.7B. Optimizer state falls from 112 GB to 640 MB, which combined with a 4-bit frozen base is what puts a 7B tune on one 24 GB consumer card.
interview_question: You raise LoRA rank from 8 to 64, memory climbs, and quality barely moves. Explain what r is actually controlling, and name the change that would have helped more.
answer_points: r bounds the rank of the update, not its magnitude — task adaptation is genuinely low-rank, so marginal gain past r≈16 is small on typical SFT data
α/r holds the effective scale fixed across r, so the LR needs no retuning; people who omit it confound rank changes with LR changes
Which modules you attach to matters more than r: attention-only can reach at most a third of the body, and adding the FFN projections usually beats doubling rank
B=0 at init is what makes attaching a LoRA anywhere safe — no warmup, no quality cliff at step 0
QLoRA's win is orthogonal to rank: it quantises the frozen base to NF4, taking 14 GB of base weights to 3.5 GB, which is the actual single-GPU enabler

concept: Bradley-Terry models the probability a human prefers y_w over y_l as σ of the reward difference, and training maximises the log-likelihood of the observed rankings. Only the difference of rewards is identified — the absolute scale and any per-prompt offset are unconstrained, so a raw reward number carries no meaning on its own. The reward model is normally the SFT policy with its unembedding swapped for a scalar head reading the final token.
example: InstructGPT trains its reward model from the 6B SFT checkpoint on roughly 33k prompts, each with K=4 to 9 completions ranked by labellers. All C(K,2) pairs from one prompt go into a single gradient step — 36 pairs at K=9 — because splitting them across batches makes each completion appear 8 times as an apparently independent example and overfits hard. Calibration: a reward gap of 1.0 predicts σ(1) = 73% preference, a gap of 3.0 predicts 95%.
interview_question: Your reward model hits 78% pairwise accuracy on held-out preferences, but PPO against it yields long, hedging answers humans dislike. Diagnose it, and say what the loss itself cannot tell you.
answer_points: Only reward differences are identified, so the scale is arbitrary — normalise per prompt before comparing anything across prompts
78% is close to the ceiling set by labeller agreement, so the RM is not undertrained; the failure is out-of-distribution generalisation
PPO drives the policy into regions the RM never saw ranked, where it extrapolates badly — that is reward hacking, and verbosity is its most common expression
Gate on RM accuracy over on-policy samples, not the static validation set, which stops being representative after a few PPO steps; and penalise length explicitly or debias the preference data

concept: Maximise reward while staying near the reference SFT policy, with β pricing the drift. The KL term is not a safety bolt-on — it is what keeps the policy inside the distribution where the reward model was actually trained and therefore still means something. The objective has a closed-form optimum, π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β), a Boltzmann tilt of the reference by the reward. That identity is exactly what DPO exploits.
example: PPO implements this by folding the KL into the per-token reward: r_t = −β·log(π_θ(y_t)/π_ref(y_t)), with the RM score added only at the final token. At β=0.02, a policy drifting 2 nats per token over a 200-token completion accumulates 400 nats of KL and pays 8 reward units back — so an RM score of 12 nets out at 4. Runs are monitored on total KL and halted past a few hundred nats, because that is where reward hacking shows up.
interview_question: Derive the optimal policy for the KL-regularised reward objective, then explain what β=0 and β→∞ each give you and how you would actually pick β.
answer_points: Optimise over the distribution π per prompt: the solution is π*(y|x) = π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β) / Z(x)
β=0 is pure reward maximisation and collapses onto whatever the RM overrates; β→∞ returns the SFT model untouched
Z(x) is intractable, which is why you cannot sample π* directly and must run PPO — or use DPO, which cancels Z by working on pairs
Do not fix β: target a KL budget instead. Adaptive-KL controllers adjust β each iteration to hold KL near target, because the right β moves as the policy does

concept: Substitute the closed-form RLHF optimum back into the Bradley-Terry likelihood and the intractable partition function Z(x) cancels, because it is identical for y_w and y_l. What is left is a supervised classification loss over preference pairs, with an implicit reward r(x,y) = β·log(π_θ/π_ref). No reward model, no sampling loop, no value network — but π_ref must still be scored on both completions.
example: Zephyr-7B was DPO-tuned from a Mistral-7B SFT base on roughly 62k UltraFeedback preference pairs at β=0.1, in a few GPU-hours. PPO needs four models resident — policy, reference, reward, value — while DPO needs two, and the reference log-probabilities can be precomputed offline once, taking it to one. At β=0.1 an implicit reward gap of 1.0 requires the policy to move its log-probability ratio by 10 nats.
interview_question: DPO removes the reward model entirely. Show where the partition function goes, then say what you give up relative to PPO and when that actually bites.
answer_points: Invert π* = π_ref·exp(r/β)/Z to get r = β·log(π_θ/π_ref) + β·log Z(x); in the Bradley-Terry difference the β·log Z terms cancel because Z depends only on x
The result is binary cross-entropy on pairs: stable, off-policy, no sampling, no value network
What is lost is on-policy exploration — DPO only sees the fixed preference set and cannot discover anything better than what is already in it

The gradient pushes log π(y_l) down as hard as it pushes log π(y_w) up, so with noisy or off-policy pairs probability mass drains to neither and the model degrades — which is why iterative/online DPO, or an added SFT term on y_w, is now standard

concept: Symmetric means zero maps to zero, so there is no zero-point and the dequantised matmul is an integer GEMM times a scale, with no cross terms to correct. Using 127 rather than 128 keeps the range symmetric about zero. The decision that actually matters is granularity: one scale per tensor is cheapest, but a single outlier sets the scale for everything, while per-channel gives one scale per output neuron for the price of a vector.
example: Take a weight row spanning [−0.42, 0.38] with one outlier at 6.1. Per-tensor: s = 6.1/127 = 0.048, so 0.38 becomes round(7.9) = 8 and the entire normal range occupies 9 of 127 levels — under 3.3 effective bits of the 8 you paid for. Per-channel puts that outlier in its own channel and the rest get s = 0.42/127 = 0.0033, using the full range. That is why per-channel weights with per-token activations is the default.
interview_question: INT8 weight-only quantisation of your 13B model is lossless, but enabling INT8 activations costs 4 points on your eval. Explain the asymmetry and describe the fix that does not drop back to fp16.
answer_points: Weights are static and well-conditioned per channel; activations are dynamic and, above roughly 6.7B parameters, develop systematic outlier channels 20–100× the typical magnitude
A per-tensor activation scale is then set by those outliers and the useful range collapses to a few effective bits
Fix with per-token dynamic activation scales, plus SmoothQuant, which migrates outlier magnitude from activations into weights through a per-channel diagonal rescale the GEMM absorbs for free
LLM.int8() instead keeps outlier channels in fp16 and runs a mixed decomposition — correct, but slower, because it breaks the single fused INT8 GEMM

concept: A draft model proposes k tokens; the target verifies all k+1 positions in one forward pass and accepts the longest prefix consistent with its own distribution. α is the per-token acceptance rate, so expected accepted length is the truncated geometric sum (1−α^(k+1))/(1−α). c is the draft's cost as a fraction of one target step, making 1+kc the cost of a verify round. Rejection sampling makes the output distribution exactly the target's — this is lossless, not an approximation.
example: α=0.8, k=4, c=0.1: expected accepted length is (1−0.8⁵)/0.2 = 3.36 tokens for a round costing 1+0.4 = 1.4 target-steps, so 2.4×. The optimum sits near k=6 at 2.47×, and by k=12 it has fallen back to 2.15×, because accepted length saturates at 1/(1−α) = 5 while cost keeps growing linearly in k. Drop α to 0.6 and k=3 yields only 2.18/1.3 = 1.7×.
interview_question: Speculative decoding gives you 2.4× at batch 1 but nothing at batch 32. Explain why the formula stops applying, and say when you would still ship it.
answer_points: Accepted length is a truncated geometric capped at 1/(1−α), so raising k has sharply diminishing returns while the draft cost kc grows linearly — there is an interior optimum
The entire win depends on decode being memory-bound: verifying k+1 positions costs about the same as verifying 1 because the target's weights are read once either way
At batch 32 the GPU is already compute-saturated, the extra verification FLOPs are no longer free, and speedup collapses toward 1 or below

It is exact rather than approximate, so it needs no quality sign-off the way quantisation does — ship it for latency-sensitive low-batch traffic, and prefer self-speculation heads like Medusa or EAGLE so there is no second model to serve

formula: \begin{gathered} AI = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}} \\[3pt] \text{compute-bound} \iff AI > AI_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{\text{peak FLOP/s}}{\text{peak bandwidth}} \end{gathered}
concept: Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs performed per byte moved from HBM. The ridge point is the hardware's peak FLOP/s divided by its peak bandwidth. A kernel below the ridge can never reach peak FLOPs however well it is written, because it starves waiting on memory; above it, memory is not the constraint. This one number decides whether an optimisation should target FLOPs or bytes — get it wrong and you optimise the side that is not binding.
example: A100 80GB: 312 TFLOP/s bf16 over 2039 GB/s gives a ridge of 153 FLOP/byte. Batch-1 fp16 decode does 2N FLOPs while moving 2N bytes of weights, so AI = 1.0 — 153× below the ridge, and the GPU delivers about 1/153 of peak. Since the weights are read once per step regardless of batch, decode AI simply equals the batch size: you need roughly 153 concurrent sequences to reach the ridge. On an H100 the ridge is 990/3.35 = 295, so the target is higher still.
interview_question: Your decode throughput sits at 1/100th of the GPU's peak FLOPs and a colleague proposes INT8 weights to 'add more compute'. Compute the arithmetic intensity, say whether they are right, and give the number that settles it.
answer_points: AI = FLOPs/bytes and ridge = peak FLOP/s ÷ peak bandwidth: 153 on an A100, about 295 on an H100
fp16 batch-1 decode has AI = 2N/2N = 1, so it is memory-bound by two orders of magnitude and adding compute changes nothing
INT8 does help, but for the memory reason not the compute one — it halves the bytes moved, doubling AI and roughly doubling decode throughput

Decode AI equals the batch size, so the highest-leverage fix is raising concurrency via continuous batching, and that is capped by KV cache capacity — which routes straight back to GQA and paged attention

concept: Time per output token in decode is set by how long it takes to stream the weights out of HBM, not by arithmetic. Each generated token requires reading every weight once, plus the KV cache of the sequences in flight. Dividing by the tensor-parallel degree splits the weights across devices, so TPOT falls roughly linearly in TP until the per-layer all-reduce starts to dominate. This is why decode latency is a bandwidth calculation.
example: LLaMA-2 70B in fp16 is 140 GB. With TP=4 on A100s each GPU holds 35 GB and streams it at about 2 TB/s: 35/2000 = 17.5 ms per token, roughly 57 tokens/s, and measured numbers land close because decode really is bandwidth-bound. At 4k context the KV cache adds 10.5 GB per sequence, 2.6 GB per GPU, taking TPOT to about 18.8 ms. A 500-token answer is then 9.4 s of decode on top of TTFT.
interview_question: A product owner wants a 70B to stream at 30 tokens per second per user and you have A100s. Work out whether it is possible, what tensor-parallel degree it needs, and what breaks first as you scale that up.
answer_points: 30 tok/s means TPOT ≤ 33 ms, so ≤66 GB may be read per GPU per token: TP=2 gives 70/2000 = 35 ms (marginal), TP=4 gives 17.5 ms comfortably
This is a bandwidth calculation, not a FLOPs one — the GPU sits at a few percent of peak compute throughout decode
TP scaling is not free: every layer ends in an all-reduce over d_model, so beyond TP=8 (one NVLink domain) the collective over PCIe or InfiniBand dominates and TPOT stops improving

Per-user TPOT and fleet throughput pull opposite ways — raising batch leaves TPOT nearly unchanged while multiplying throughput — so quote both, and note TPOT drifts upward within a request as its KV cache grows

concept: Prefill processes the entire prompt in one pass, so it is compute-bound: S tokens at 2N FLOPs each. Substituting N = 12Ld² for the body gives the second form. Effective throughput is peak times MFU, and prefill achieves high MFU precisely because each layer is one large GEMM. Unlike decode, TTFT grows linearly in prompt length — until attention's S² term becomes a material share of the total.
example: LLaMA-2 7B on one A100 at 312 TFLOP/s and 50% MFU, so 156 TFLOP/s effective. A 512-token prompt is 2·7×10⁹·512 = 7.2 TFLOPs → 46 ms. A 2048-token prompt is 4× that, 29 TFLOPs → 184 ms. The neglected attention term scales as S/(6·d_model) = 2048/24576 ≈ 8% at 2k, rising to 33% at 8k — so linearity is a good approximation to a few thousand tokens and then bends upward.
interview_question: TTFT is 180 ms at 2k prompts against a 200 ms SLA, and users have started pasting 8k documents. Predict the new TTFT, then propose two ways to hold the SLA that do not involve buying more GPUs.
answer_points: The linear term scales 4×, 184 ms → 736 ms, and the attention S² term grows from 8% to 33% of the total, putting it near 950 ms
Prefill is compute-bound and already at high MFU, so there is no per-request efficiency headroom left to reclaim
Prefix caching removes prefill entirely for shared system prompts and repeated documents; chunked prefill splits a long prompt so it interleaves with decode instead of blocking the batch

The structural fix is disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate pools — they have opposite bottlenecks, so co-locating them lets one long prefill stall every decode in flight, which appears as SLA misses under load and never in single-request benchmarks

concept: FlashAttention never materialises the N×N attention matrix in HBM. It tiles Q, K and V into blocks sized for on-chip SRAM, computes the softmax online with a running maximum and running normaliser, and rescales the accumulated output as each new K/V block arrives. M is the SRAM size, so larger on-chip memory means fewer passes over K and V. The result is numerically exact, not an approximation.
example: One head at N=2048, d_h=64, fp16. Standard attention materialises a 2048×2048 score matrix — 8.4 MB — and writes then re-reads it for the softmax, moving roughly 33 MB per head. FlashAttention tiles into the A100's 192 KB of per-SM shared memory and moves only Q, K, V and O: 4·2048·64·2 bytes = 1.0 MB, about 30× less. It does slightly more arithmetic and is still far faster.
interview_question: FlashAttention is often described as making attention O(N) in memory. State precisely what is O(N) and what is not, then explain why it wins on wall clock despite doing strictly more arithmetic.
answer_points: Memory is O(N) because the N×N score matrix is never materialised; FLOPs stay Θ(N²d) and actually rise slightly, because the backward pass recomputes scores
Attention at these shapes is memory-bound, so trading extra FLOPs for far fewer HBM round-trips is a straight win
The mechanism is the online softmax: a running max for stability plus a running normaliser, with the accumulated output rescaled as each K/V block is consumed

The backward pass also avoids the N×N matrix by recomputing it from saved softmax statistics — which is why the saving holds during training, not just inference — and FA2's gain came mostly from re-partitioning work across warps, not from the tiling idea itself

concept: f_i is the fraction of tokens in the batch actually routed to expert i; p_i is the mean router probability assigned to expert i. The sum is scaled by n so its minimum is exactly 1 under uniform routing. f_i is not differentiable — it comes from a discrete top-k — so gradient flows only through p_i, nudging the router away from experts already taking too much traffic. Without this term routing collapses onto a handful of experts and the rest never train.
example: Switch Transformer with n=64 experts, top-1 routing, α=0.01. Uniform routing gives f_i = p_i = 1/64, so L_aux = 0.01·64·64·(1/64)² = 0.01, the floor. If one expert captures 50% of tokens its term alone contributes 64·0.5·0.5 = 16, taking L_aux to 0.163 — 16× the floor. α=0.01 is chosen small enough not to distort a language-modelling loss of 2 to 4 nats, yet large enough to move the router logits.
interview_question: Your MoE trains stably but two of 64 experts absorb 40% of tokens, and eval is worse than a dense model with the same active parameter count. Diagnose it, and say what the auxiliary loss can and cannot fix.
answer_points: L_aux bottoms out at α under the n scaling, so plot the actual f_i histogram against the 1/n floor before changing anything
The gradient reaches p_i only, since f_i comes from a non-differentiable top-k — the loss shapes router probabilities, it never moves assignments directly
α too small leaves the collapse in place; too large and the router balances by sending tokens to experts that are wrong for them, which is exactly the eval regression you are seeing
Capacity factor is the other half of the story: tokens over an expert's capacity are dropped and pass through the residual unchanged, so a healthy f_i histogram can still hide heavy dropping
DeepSeek-V3 removes the aux loss entirely in favour of a per-expert routing bias adjusted online, precisely because the aux gradient fights the language-modelling objective

formula: \frac{\partial s_i}{\partial x_j} = s_i\,(\delta_{ij} - s_j), \qquad J = \mathrm{diag}(s) - s\,s^{\top}
concept: The softmax Jacobian is a dense n×n matrix, because the normaliser couples every output to every input. Diagonal entries are s_i(1−s_i), off-diagonal entries −s_i s_j. Two consequences follow: the Jacobian is singular, since outputs are constrained to sum to 1 so every row sums to zero; and it collapses toward zero as s approaches one-hot, which is exactly the saturation that kills gradients in unscaled attention logits.
example: For s = [0.7, 0.2, 0.1]: ∂s₁/∂x₁ = 0.7·0.3 = 0.21 and ∂s₁/∂x₂ = −0.7·0.2 = −0.14. Now take s = [0.99, 0.005, 0.005]: the same diagonal entry collapses to 0.99·0.01 = 0.0099, 21× smaller. Composed with cross-entropy the algebra telescopes to dL/dx = s − y, so a confidently wrong prediction still returns a gradient of magnitude near 1 — the saturation cancels exactly.
interview_question: Derive dL/dx for a softmax followed by cross-entropy, then explain why frameworks fuse the two into a single op instead of composing their backward passes.
answer_points: ∂s_i/∂x_j = s_i(δ_ij − s_j), giving J = diag(s) − ssᵀ, dense because the normaliser couples all outputs
With L = −Σ y_i log s_i the Jacobian-vector product telescopes to dL/dx = s − y — an O(n) vector rather than an O(n²) matrix
Fusing avoids ever forming that Jacobian: at a 50257-token vocabulary it would be 2.5 billion entries per token

Fusion is also a numerical fix — log-sum-exp with the max subtracted keeps log s finite, whereas taking softmax then its log underflows to −∞ on confidently wrong tokens, which is precisely when the gradient matters most

concept: The expectation is taken over training sets, not over test points — that is the part people get wrong. Bias is how far the average model across resampled training sets sits from the truth; variance is how much the fitted model moves as that training set is resampled; σ² is label noise no model can beat. The identity is exact for squared error only, which is why bias-variance is a mental model in classification rather than a theorem.
example: Fit degree-1 to degree-15 polynomials to 20 points drawn from a degree-3 truth with σ=0.5, so σ²=0.25. Degree 1: train MSE 2.0, test MSE 2.1 — a small gap, both bad, bias-dominated. Degree 15: train MSE 0.02 while test MSE climbs to 4.8, almost entirely variance. Degree 3 lands near test MSE 0.27, just above the 0.25 floor. That floor is the signal to stop: no capacity and no extra data drives MSE below 0.25 here.
interview_question: A model shows 2% training error and 12% validation error, and your junior wants to add capacity. Decompose the 10-point gap, say what you would do first, and state the number that tells you the ceiling.
answer_points: A large train-validation gap is the signature of variance, and added capacity raises variance — it makes this worse, not better
First moves are the ones that cut variance without raising bias: more data, stronger regularisation, bagging, early stopping
Estimate the irreducible error from the label-noise rate or human agreement on the same examples, because that is the floor and it bounds what any fix can buy

The exact three-term split holds for squared error only; under 0-1 loss the analogue is not additive, and in the overparameterised regime test error can descend a second time past the interpolation threshold — so the classic U-curve is not a safe guide for a large network

concept: n is per arm. Δ is the minimum detectable effect you commit to before running, σ² the per-unit variance of the metric, and the two z terms encode the false-positive rate α and the power 1−β. The leading 2 appears because you are estimating a difference between two independent means. The shape that matters: n scales with 1/Δ², so halving the effect you want to catch quadruples the sample you need.
example: Two-sided α=0.05 gives z=1.96 and 80% power gives z=0.84, so (1.96+0.84)² = 7.85. For a conversion metric at p=0.10, σ² = p(1−p) = 0.09. Detecting a relative 5% lift means Δ=0.005, so n = 2·0.09·7.85/0.005² = 56,500 per arm. Chase a 2% lift instead and Δ=0.002 gives 353,000 per arm — 6.25× the traffic for an effect only 2.5× smaller.
interview_question: Product wants to ship after an experiment that ran 3 days and showed a 4% lift at p=0.06. Compute what it would have taken to call that reliably, and list what you would check before saying no.
answer_points: n scales as σ²/Δ² times (z_{1−α/2} + z_{1−β})² = 7.85 at α=0.05 and 80% power — plug in the observed baseline variance and compare against what they actually collected
An underpowered test landing near significance is the winner's curse: conditional on crossing the threshold, the observed effect overstates the true one
Check for peeking — repeatedly evaluating inflates the false-positive rate well beyond 5%, and the fix is sequential testing or always-valid confidence intervals, not a stricter p

Three days misses the weekly cycle, and randomising by user while measuring per session breaks the independence assumption, so σ² is underestimated and the whole calculation is optimistic; use CUPED to cut σ² with pre-experiment covariates rather than only running longer

formula: \begin{gathered} C = AB: \quad 2mnk \ \text{FLOPs} \\[3pt] 2(mk + kn + mn)\ \text{bytes in fp16} \end{gathered}
concept: Almost everything in a transformer is a matmul plus an elementwise op, so the shape of the matmul decides the hardware efficiency. For A [m×k] times B [k×n] the cost is 2mnk FLOPs against roughly 2(mk+kn+mn) bytes in fp16, giving an arithmetic intensity near mnk/(mk+kn+mn). Large square matmuls sit far above a GPU's ridge point and run near peak; thin ones sit far below it and stall on memory. Same algebra, wildly different throughput.
example: A 4096×4096 by 4096×4096 fp16 matmul: 2·4096³ = 137 GFLOPs moving 3·4096²·2 = 100 MB, an intensity of about 1370 FLOP/byte — far above an A100's ridge of 153, so it is compute-bound and runs near peak. Now the same weight against a single vector: 2·4096² = 34 MFLOPs against 33 MB, intensity 1.0, memory-bound at roughly 1/150 of peak. That precise gap is prefill versus decode.
interview_question: You replace one batched matmul with a loop of matrix-vector products. The FLOP count is identical but it runs about 100× slower. Explain why, with numbers.
answer_points: FLOPs are equal but bytes moved are not — batching amortises reading the weight matrix across every vector in the batch
Intensity for m×k by k×n is ≈ mnk/(mk+kn+mn); at n=1 that collapses to about 1 FLOP/byte
Compare to the ridge point (A100: 312 TFLOP/s ÷ 2039 GB/s = 153) — below it no kernel, however good, reaches peak
This is exactly why decode batches requests: the weights are read once per step regardless of how many sequences share that read

concept: MLE picks the parameters that make the observed data most likely. Taking a log turns the product into a sum and negating gives the loss you actually minimise — which is why cross-entropy is not merely analogous to maximum likelihood but identical to it under a categorical model. MAP adds a prior, and a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights is exactly L2 regularisation. The Gaussian MLE for σ² divides by n and is biased low, because the same data already supplied the estimate of μ.
example: Fit a Gaussian to n=5 samples [2,4,4,4,5]. MLE gives μ̂ = 3.8 and σ̂² = (1/5)·4.80 = 0.96, while the unbiased estimator divides by n−1 = 4 for 1.20 — 25% larger. The bias is exactly σ²/n, so it vanishes at scale and bites at n=5. The same MLE logic on tokens gives NLL = −(1/N)Σ log p(x_i), which is cross-entropy: a uniform guess over 50257 tokens costs ln 50257 = 10.82 nats.
interview_question: A colleague claims cross-entropy loss and maximum likelihood are different things, and that weight decay is just a training trick with no principled basis. Correct both claims.
answer_points: Maximising Π p(x_i|θ) is the same problem as minimising −Σ log p(x_i|θ); dividing by N makes it cross-entropy exactly
MAP maximises p(θ|D) ∝ p(D|θ)·p(θ), and a zero-mean Gaussian prior contributes −λ‖θ‖² to the log posterior — that is L2, derived rather than invented
So weight decay has a precise Bayesian reading as a Gaussian prior over weights

AdamW deliberately breaks that equivalence: decoupling decay from the adaptive step means it is no longer exactly Gaussian MAP, but it works better because Adam's per-parameter scaling otherwise distorts the penalty unevenly across parameters

formula: \begin{gathered} \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial r} \cdot \frac{\partial r}{\partial W} \\[3pt] L = \|Wx - y\|^2 \ \Rightarrow\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = 2\,r\,x^{\top} \end{gathered}
concept: Backprop is the multivariate chain rule evaluated right to left. Reverse mode accumulates a vector-Jacobian product at each step and never materialises the Jacobian itself. Direction is the whole trick: forward mode costs one pass per input, reverse mode one pass per output, and with a single scalar loss and billions of parameters, reverse wins by that same enormous factor. Shapes are the practical sanity check — dL/dW always has the shape of W, which catches most sign and transpose errors immediately.
example: L = ‖Wx − y‖² with W [m×n]. Let r = Wx − y, so L = rᵀr, dL/dr = 2r, and dL/dW = 2r xᵀ — an outer product of shape [m×n], matching W. Concretely W = [[1,2],[3,4]], x = [1,1], y = [2,5]: Wx = [3,7], r = [1,2], and dL/dW = 2·[1,2]ᵀ[1,1] = [[2,2],[4,4]]. If your derivation produces an [n×m], you have transposed something.
interview_question: A junior asks why backprop is called reverse-mode and whether forward-mode autodiff would work just as well. Answer with the cost argument, then say when forward mode genuinely is the right choice.
answer_points: Reverse mode computes vᵀJ at one pass per output; forward mode computes Jv at one pass per input
Training has one scalar loss against ~10⁹ parameters, so reverse is cheaper by that ratio — the asymmetry is the entire justification
The price is memory: reverse must retain forward activations until the backward pass consumes them, which is exactly what activation checkpointing trades back for recompute
Forward mode wins when outputs vastly outnumber inputs — a handful of hyperparameters, or directional derivatives where you want Jv for one specific v

formula: \begin{gathered} p(y=1 \mid x) = \sigma(w^{\top}x + b) \\[3pt] \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (\sigma(z) - y)\,x \end{gathered}
concept: Logistic regression models the log-odds as linear in x and is fit by maximising the Bernoulli likelihood, which is precisely binary cross-entropy. The gradient is remarkably clean — prediction minus target, times the input — the same form that reappears in softmax with cross-entropy. The objective is convex, so there is one global optimum. L2 is what keeps the fit finite when classes are perfectly separable: without it ‖w‖ diverges as the model pushes σ toward exactly 0 and 1.
example: One feature, w=0.5, b=0, x=2, y=1. Then z=1.0, σ(1)=0.731, loss = −ln 0.731 = 0.313, and the gradient is (0.731−1)·2 = −0.538. One SGD step at lr=0.1 gives w=0.554, z=1.108, σ=0.752, loss 0.285. On perfectly separable data with no L2, repeating this drives w→∞ and loss→0 while accuracy stops improving after the first correct split.
interview_question: Your logistic regression hits 100% training accuracy, the weights keep growing every epoch, and validation AUC slowly drifts down. Explain the mechanism and give the one-line fix.
answer_points: Perfect separability means the likelihood is only maximised in the limit ‖w‖→∞, so gradient descent never converges and keeps inflating the margin
Adding L2 makes the objective strictly convex with a finite optimum — that is the one-line fix
The gradient (σ(z)−y)x shrinks as σ saturates, so the process slows but never halts on its own
Growing ‖w‖ also destroys calibration: probabilities collapse toward 0 and 1, so if you need usable scores you want Platt scaling or isotonic regression on a held-out split, not merely early stopping

concept: L1 and L2 differ in the geometry of their constraint region. The L2 ball is round, so a loss contour almost never touches it on an axis and coefficients shrink smoothly toward but never onto zero. The L1 ball has corners on the axes, and corners are exactly where a generic contour makes first contact — so solutions land on axes and coefficients become exactly zero. Equivalently: L1's subgradient is a constant ±λ that does not vanish near zero, while L2's is 2λw and does.
example: Ridge on one feature shrinks proportionally: ŵ = w/(1+λ), so 0.8 becomes 0.4 at λ=1 and 0.08 at λ=9 — small, never zero. Lasso soft-thresholds instead: at λ=0.5, 0.8 becomes 0.3 and anything under 0.5 becomes exactly 0. On a 1000-feature problem with 20 real signals, that is the difference between 980 exact zeros and 980 small non-zeros you still have to threshold by hand.
interview_question: You have 1000 features, 200 samples, and you need to know which features actually matter. Compare L1 and L2 for that goal, then describe how you would validate the choice without fooling yourself.
answer_points: L1's constraint region has corners on the axes so the optimum lands there, producing exact zeros; L2's is smooth and gives shrinkage without selection
Subgradient view: L1's penalty gradient is ±λ regardless of magnitude, L2's is 2λw and vanishes as w→0
With p ≫ n, L1 selects at most n features and picks arbitrarily among correlated ones — reach for elastic net when that grouping matters
Selecting features and tuning λ on the same split leaks badly: use nested CV with selection inside the inner loop, or your reported error is optimistic by a wide and unknowable margin

formula: \begin{gathered} do = p - y, \qquad dW_2 = h^{\top}do, \qquad dh = do\,W_2^{\top} \\[3pt] dz_1 = dh \odot \mathbb{1}[z_1 > 0], \qquad dW_1 = x^{\top}dz_1 \end{gathered}
concept: Forward is function composition; backward applies the chain rule in reverse while reusing every stored intermediate. For h = ReLU(xW₁+b₁) and o = hW₂+b₂ under softmax cross-entropy, the whole backward pass is five lines. ReLU's derivative is just a mask, which is why it is cheap — and also why dead units never recover: a unit whose pre-activation is negative on every example receives exactly zero gradient, permanently.
example: Batch 32, input 2, hidden 8, output 2 on XOR. W₁ is 2×8 = 16 params, W₂ is 8×2 = 16, plus 10 biases: 42 weights total. The forward stores x [32×2], z₁ [32×8] and p [32×2] — 384 floats of activations against those 42 weights. Even at this toy scale activations dominate memory by 9×, which is the same ratio that forces activation checkpointing on real models. Gradient-check with (L(w+1e-5)−L(w−1e-5))/2e-5 and expect ~1e-7 relative agreement.
interview_question: Your numpy 2-layer net trains on XOR but the loss plateaus at 0.69 and half the hidden units output zero for every input. Diagnose it and give two fixes.
answer_points: 0.69 is ln 2 — the model is outputting 50/50 and has learned nothing at all
Dead ReLUs: the mask 1[z>0] is zero for those units on every example, so their columns of dW₁ are identically zero and cannot recover
Usual causes are too large a learning rate driving a large negative bias update, or poor init; fixes are lower LR, He initialisation, or LeakyReLU/GELU which keep a non-zero slope for negatives
Run a gradient check before blaming optimisation — a sign or transpose error in dz₁ = dh ⊙ mask produces this exact symptom, and no amount of LR tuning will fix it

formula: \begin{gathered} A = U\Sigma V^{\top} \\[3pt] \|A - A_r\|_F \ \text{minimised by the top } r\ \sigma_i \quad \text{(Eckart–Young)} \end{gathered}
concept: SVD factors any matrix into UΣVᵀ, where the singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA. Truncating to the top r gives the provably best rank-r approximation in both Frobenius and spectral norm. PCA is just SVD of the centred data matrix: principal directions are the right singular vectors and explained variance is σᵢ²/Σσⱼ². The same idea underlies LoRA — asserting that a fine-tuning update is well approximated at small rank is asserting its spectrum decays fast.
example: A 4096×4096 weight matrix holds 16.8M parameters. A rank-16 truncation stores U [4096×16] and ΣVᵀ [16×4096] — 131k parameters, a 128× reduction, which is exactly LoRA's arithmetic at r=16. Whether that is lossless depends entirely on the spectrum: if the top 16 singular values carry 95% of Σσ² it is nearly free, but for a pretrained weight matrix they typically carry far less.
interview_question: Someone proposes shrinking your model by replacing every weight matrix with its rank-16 SVD truncation, citing LoRA as the precedent. Evaluate the proposal.
answer_points: Eckart–Young says truncation is optimal for a given rank, so the method is sound — the real question is whether the spectrum justifies r=16
Pretrained weight matrices are typically near full rank with slowly decaying spectra, so rank-16 discards a great deal
LoRA's claim is that ΔW, the update, is low-rank — not that W itself is; conflating the two is the actual error here
Even where accuracy survives, a rank-r factorisation replaces one GEMM with two smaller ones, which is usually slower on tensor cores at these shapes, so a memory win can cost latency

concept: ReLU is cheap, non-saturating above zero, and its derivative is a mask — but a unit whose pre-activation is always negative gets zero gradient forever. GELU multiplies the input by the probability a standard normal falls below it, so small negatives pass through attenuated instead of being clipped. SiLU is nearly the same curve using a sigmoid gate and is cheaper to evaluate. Both are non-monotonic near zero, which is what lets them act as soft gates rather than hard switches.
example: At x = [−2,−1,0,1,2]: ReLU gives [0,0,0,1,2]. GELU gives [−0.045,−0.159,0,0.841,1.955]. SiLU gives [−0.238,−0.269,0,0.731,1.762]. Both retain a small negative response near x=−1 where ReLU is flat zero, and both recover to nearly identity by x=2. SiLU's minimum is about −0.278 at x≈−1.28 — that dip is the non-monotonicity, and it is what SwiGLU wraps in a gated linear unit.
interview_question: A teammate swaps GELU for ReLU in a transformer FFN to save compute. The model still trains but final loss is slightly worse. Explain what was actually lost and whether the trade makes sense.
answer_points: ReLU zeroes all negatives and discards that sign information; GELU and SiLU pass small negatives attenuated, giving a smoother loss surface and live gradients there
GELU has a stochastic-regulariser reading: x·Φ(x) is the expected value of x under a Bernoulli gate firing with probability Φ(x)
The compute saving is negligible — FFN cost is the two GEMMs, not the elementwise nonlinearity, which is memory-bound and normally fused into a neighbouring kernel
So the trade fails for the very reason it looked attractive: the activation was never on the critical path, and ReLU's induced sparsity only pays off with kernels that actually exploit it

concept: The naive form overflows as soon as any logit exceeds about 88 in float32, because e^x passes the largest representable value. Subtracting max(x) before exponentiating changes nothing mathematically — the constant cancels between numerator and denominator — while guaranteeing the largest exponent is e⁰ = 1 and the rest underflow harmlessly toward zero. Log-softmax goes one step further, computing x − logsumexp(x) directly so the logarithm is never applied to an underflowed zero.
example: x = [1000, 1001, 1002] in float32: naive exp gives [inf, inf, inf], then inf/inf = NaN and the batch is lost. Subtracting the max gives [−2,−1,0] → exp [0.135, 0.368, 1.0], sum 1.503, softmax [0.090, 0.245, 0.665] — correct. Separately, log(softmax(x)) on a confidently wrong token underflows to log(0) = −inf, whereas logsumexp keeps it finite at about −2.41.
interview_question: Training loss goes to NaN at step 3000, always in the same layer, and only in fp16. Walk through how you would isolate it and name the two most likely causes.
answer_points: fp16 maxes out at 65504 and exp overflows above an exponent of roughly 11, so unnormalised logits are the first suspect — log max|logit| per layer per step
Softmax without max-subtraction, or with the subtraction itself done in fp16, gives inf/inf = NaN
The other classic is a normaliser underflowing to zero and then being divided by — check that ε sits inside the sqrt, not outside
Also check the attention mask: −1e9 instead of −inf overflows fp16 to −inf, and a fully masked row then produces NaN even though the softmax code is correct

formula: \begin{gathered} L = -\sum_i y_i \log p_i = -\log p_{\text{correct}} \\[3pt] \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{logits}} = p - y \end{gathered}
concept: Against a one-hot target, cross-entropy collapses to minus the log probability of the correct class, because every other term is multiplied by zero. That is why the loss only ever sees the probability assigned to the right token. Fused with softmax, the gradient on the logits is simply p − y: a confident correct prediction contributes almost nothing, a confident wrong one contributes magnitude near 1. That self-balancing property is why the two are never implemented as separate ops.
example: Three classes, logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1], target class 0. Softmax gives [0.659, 0.242, 0.099], loss = −ln 0.659 = 0.417, and the gradient on logits is [−0.341, 0.242, 0.099], summing to zero as it must. Apply label smoothing at 0.1 and the target becomes [0.933, 0.033, 0.033], so the gradient never fully vanishes and the model is actively discouraged from driving p to exactly 1.
interview_question: Your classifier reaches 99% training accuracy but its predicted probabilities are useless for downstream thresholding. Explain what cross-entropy did and did not optimise, and what you would change.
answer_points: CE is a proper scoring rule so it does reward calibration, but nothing stops it pushing p→1 once the data is separable, which produces systematic overconfidence
The gradient p − y shrinks as p→1, so confident-correct examples stop contributing and only residual errors keep driving training
Label smoothing caps achievable confidence and keeps a gradient alive; temperature scaling on a held-out set fixes calibration afterwards with a single parameter and no retraining

Decide first whether you need calibration or ranking — smoothing improves ECE but can hurt AUC, and it degrades the model as a distillation teacher because it deliberately flattens the dark-knowledge structure in the tail

concept: Adam keeps per-parameter first and second moment estimates and divides each step by √v, so every parameter gets a step scaled to its own gradient history. Bias correction matters because m and v start at zero and would otherwise be biased toward zero for hundreds of steps. AdamW's change is small and consequential: L2 added to the loss flows through the gradient and gets divided by √v like everything else, so parameters with large gradients receive less decay. Decoupling applies λθ straight to the weight instead.
example: β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, first step with g=0.1: m₁=0.01 and v₁=1e-5. Uncorrected the step would be 0.01/√1e-5 = 3.16 — 30× too large. Corrected, m̂=0.1 and v̂=1e-2, giving 0.1/0.1 = 1.0, the intended unit step. Memory: m and v are 4 bytes each per parameter, so a 7B model pays 56 GB for optimiser state alone, before weights and gradients.
interview_question: You switch Adam to AdamW at identical learning rate and weight decay, change nothing else, and the model generalises noticeably better. Explain precisely what changed in the update rule.
answer_points: In Adam, L2 enters through the gradient and is divided by √v̂ with everything else, so parameters with large historical gradients are systematically decayed less
AdamW applies λθ directly to the weight, outside the adaptive scaling, making decay uniform across parameters
It also decouples the hyperparameters: in Adam the effective decay scales with the learning rate, so tuning one silently retunes the other
A consequence worth knowing: Adam's L2 is no longer a Gaussian prior in the MAP sense, and the practical tell is that the best λ under AdamW is often 10–100× the value that worked under Adam

concept: Warmup exists because Adam's second-moment estimate is unreliable in the first few hundred steps: v is built from very few samples, so 1/√v̂ can be enormous and a full-size step can move weights somewhere unrecoverable. Ramping the learning rate limits the damage while v stabilises. Cosine decay then holds a moderate rate for most of the budget and anneals smoothly to near zero, which beats step decay empirically — the model needs a long low-rate tail to settle.
example: For a 1000-step run with warmup=100, max_lr=3e-4, min_lr=3e-5: the rate rises linearly from 0 to 3e-4 over the first 100 steps, passes 1.65e-4 at step 550 (halfway through the decay, where cos = 0), and lands on 3e-5 at step 1000. The classic bug is mismatching T with the real step count — set T=1000 and train 2000 steps and the cosine argument passes π, so the learning rate climbs back up.
interview_question: You drop warmup to save 100 steps. The run diverges within 50 steps under Adam, but the identical config trains fine under plain SGD. Explain the difference.
answer_points: Adam divides by √v̂, and at step 1 that is estimated from a single gradient, so the denominator is close to meaningless and the effective step is uncontrolled
SGD has no adaptive denominator — its first step is just lr·g, which is bounded and safe
Warmup keeps steps small while v accumulates enough samples to be a usable variance estimate
The alternative is fixing the estimator rather than the schedule: RAdam rectifies the variance term, and raising β₂ or ε achieves part of the same effect — warmup is the crude but dependable option

formula: \begin{gathered} x_L = x_l + \sum_{i=l}^{L-1} F(x_i) \\[3pt] \frac{\partial x_L}{\partial x_l} = 1 + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_l}\sum_{i=l}^{L-1} F(x_i) \end{gathered}
concept: A residual connection makes a layer compute x + F(x) instead of F(x), so the Jacobian between any two depths carries an explicit identity term. Gradients then reach early layers along a path that is never multiplied down, however small the learned Jacobians are. Without it the gradient at layer l is a product of L−l Jacobians, and if their typical singular value is even slightly under 1 that product vanishes exponentially with depth. The residual converts a product into a sum.
example: Take 48 layers whose Jacobians each have typical singular value 0.9. Without residuals the gradient reaching layer 1 is scaled by 0.9⁴⁸ = 0.0064, a 156× attenuation; at 0.8 it is 0.8⁴⁸ = 2.2×10⁻⁵ and those layers effectively stop learning. With residuals the same path carries a 1 plus those terms, so the floor stays at 1 no matter the depth.
interview_question: A colleague proposes stripping residual connections from a 48-layer model to save memory, arguing modern initialisation makes them unnecessary. Quantify what breaks.
answer_points: dx_L/dx_l contains an explicit +1, so gradients reach layer 0 unattenuated; removing it makes the path a product of 48 Jacobians
At a typical singular value of 0.9 that product is 0.9⁴⁸ ≈ 0.0064, and at 0.8 it is 2×10⁻⁵ — the early layers stop training in any useful sense
The premise is also wrong on its own terms: a residual add is elementwise and can be done in place, so it costs essentially no memory
Careful depth-scaled initialisation (Fixup, T-Fixup) genuinely can train deep nets without residuals, but it is fragile and nobody ships it, precisely because the residual is free

concept: Cross-entropy decomposes exactly into the data's own entropy plus the KL divergence from model to data. H(p) is fixed by the corpus and unbeatable, so training only ever drives KL toward zero — which is why the loss has a hard floor and why comparing raw loss across datasets means nothing. KL is asymmetric, and the direction matters: forward KL is mass-covering and is what maximum likelihood minimises, reverse KL is mode-seeking and is what appears in the RLHF objective.
example: Take p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125], so H(p) = 1.75 bits. A model predicting uniform q = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] has H(p,q) = 2 bits, hence KL = 0.25 bits and perplexity 2² = 4 against the achievable 2^1.75 = 3.36. No model can score below 1.75 bits here, so a team reporting 1.6 has a bug or a leak — a cheap check worth running before anyone celebrates.
interview_question: Two teams report language-model loss on different corpora, 2.1 and 2.6 nats, and the first claims the better model. What is wrong with that comparison, and what would you ask for instead?
answer_points: Cross-entropy is H(p) + KL(p‖q), and H(p) is a property of the corpus — a lower number can simply mean an easier dataset
Only the KL term reflects model quality, and it cannot be separated without knowing H(p), so insist on a shared held-out set
Tokenisers also change the per-token normalisation, so ask for bits per byte, which is tokeniser-independent

Forward versus reverse KL is a modelling decision, not a technicality: MLE minimises forward KL and spreads mass over everything the data does, while RLHF's reverse-KL term is mode-seeking — part of why aligned models produce lower-diversity output

concept: BPE starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, recording each merge in an ordered list. Encoding replays that list in the same order, which is what makes it deterministic and exactly reversible. Vocabulary size is a direct trade: a larger vocabulary means fewer tokens per document, so shorter sequences and cheaper attention, but a bigger embedding matrix and more rarely-updated rows. There is no out-of-vocabulary case, because characters are always the fallback.
example: On 'low lower newest widest' the early merges are the frequent adjacent pairs — e+s, then es+t, since both 'newest' and 'widest' share that ending. On real vocabularies the trade is concrete: GPT-2 uses 50257 tokens at d=768, so its embedding is 38.6M params, 31% of the 124M model. LLaMA-3 moved to 128k tokens, cutting tokens per document appreciably while making that matrix 2.5× wider.
interview_question: Your team wants to move from a 32k to a 128k vocabulary to shorten sequences. Work through what that actually costs and what it gains.
answer_points: Fewer tokens per document shortens S, and attention is quadratic in S, so long-context cost falls faster than linearly
Both the embedding and the output head scale with V: at d=4096, going 32k→128k adds about 96k·4096 = 393M params per matrix
The softmax over the vocabulary gets 4× wider, which is often the peak-memory operation in the training step
Rare tokens in a large vocabulary receive very few gradient updates, so their embeddings stay near initialisation — this is the origin of glitch tokens, a genuine failure mode rather than a curiosity

concept: BPE merges by raw frequency. WordPiece merges the pair that most increases corpus likelihood under a unigram model, which reduces to a pointwise-mutual-information-style score — it prefers pairs that co-occur above chance rather than pairs that are merely common. Unigram LM runs the other direction: start from a large candidate vocabulary and prune the tokens whose removal costs the least likelihood. SentencePiece is not an algorithm but a wrapper that treats input as a raw stream including spaces, so it needs no pretokeniser.
example: BERT marks continuations with '##', so 'playing' becomes ['play', '##ing'] and a token's identity depends on whether it began a word. GPT-2 instead folds the leading space into the token, making ' play' and 'play' two different ids out of its 50257. That is why a prompt ending in a trailing space measurably degrades output — you have forced the model onto the rare, unnatural branch.
interview_question: A prompt template ends with 'Answer: ' and quality is noticeably worse than the same template without that trailing space. Explain the tokenisation cause and the fix.
answer_points: GPT-style BPE attaches the leading space to the following token, so ' Answer' and 'Answer' are distinct ids and a lone trailing space is a rare token
Ending on that space forces continuation from a distribution the model almost never saw, since in natural text the space belongs to the next word
The fix is to strip trailing whitespace and let the model emit the space as part of its own first token

This is the same class of problem token healing solves — serving stacks that implement it re-tokenise the boundary automatically, which is why an identical prompt can behave differently across frameworks

concept: The embedding matrix maps token ids to vectors; the output head maps hidden states back to vocabulary logits. Both are V×d, so tying them halves that count and, more importantly, makes a token's input and output representations the same vector — gradients arrive from both the input side and the prediction side onto one set of rows, which helps rare tokens learn faster. Some implementations scale embeddings by √d on input so their variance matches the residual stream.
example: GPT-2 small ties them: V=50257 and d=768 give a 38.6M-parameter shared matrix inside a 124M model, 31% of the total. Untying would add another 38.6M and push the model to 163M for no measured gain. The effect shrinks with scale — at GPT-3's d=12288 the embedding is 617M against 175B, so tying saves 0.35%, which is why large models often leave them untied.
interview_question: You are training a 350M model on a 128k vocabulary and someone proposes untying the embeddings for extra capacity. Evaluate the proposal.
answer_points: At V=128k the embedding dominates: with d=1024 it is 131M params, so untying adds 131M to a 350M model — a 37% increase spent entirely on vocabulary
Tying also couples input and output gradients for the same token, which matters most for rare tokens that appear seldom on either side alone
Untying is defensible at large d, where the embedding is a small fraction of the model — that is why frontier models frequently do it
At this ratio the better move is neither: shrink the vocabulary or factorise the embedding as V×k then k×d, because untying spends parameters exactly where the model is least compute-efficient

concept: Skip-gram with negative sampling replaces the full softmax over the vocabulary with a binary decision: tell a real context pair apart from k sampled noise pairs. That turns an O(V) update into O(k). Noise is drawn proportional to frequency raised to 0.75 rather than frequency itself, which upsamples rare words relative to their true rate. Levy and Goldberg showed the objective implicitly factorises a shifted PMI matrix, which is the link to GloVe's explicit factorisation of log co-occurrence counts.
example: At V=50257 a full softmax needs 50257 dot products per update; with k=5 negatives it needs 6 — roughly 8400× less work, which is what made billion-token training feasible in 2013. The 0.75 exponent has a concrete effect: for words at relative frequency 1e-2 and 1e-5, raw sampling would be 1000:1, but f^0.75 makes it 1000^0.75 = 178:1, so the rare word is drawn 5.6× more often in relative terms.
interview_question: Someone proposes Word2Vec embeddings as features for a text classifier instead of a transformer encoder. When is that defensible, and what specifically do you give up?
answer_points: You give up context — one vector per word type, so 'bank' averages the river and finance senses regardless of the sentence
SGNS implicitly factorises a shifted PMI matrix, so it captures corpus-level co-occurrence, not composition or word order
It is defensible when cost or latency dominates and the task is topical: an embedding lookup is effectively free against a full forward pass

The f^0.75 noise distribution is a real hyperparameter rather than a constant — it governs how much rare-word signal survives, and the default is often wrong for domain corpora with heavy-tailed vocabularies

formula: \begin{gathered} Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times S \times d_h} \\[3pt] QK^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times S \times S} \end{gathered}
concept: Q, K and V are three separate projections of the same residual stream. The query says what a position is looking for, the key advertises what each position offers, and the value is what actually gets copied forward. The score matrix holds one row per query position over all key positions, so causal masking sets the strictly upper triangle to −∞ before the softmax and exactly zero after — which is what lets every position train in parallel while each still sees only its own prefix.
example: Batch 4, 12 heads, S=1024, d_h=64. Q, K and V are each [4,12,1024,64] = 3.1M elements, while the score matrix is [4,12,1024,1024] = 50M elements, or 100 MB in fp16 — 16× larger than the tensors that produced it. At S=4096 that ratio becomes 64×. That single number is why FlashAttention exists.
