interview_question: Walk me through the tensor shapes in one attention layer at batch 4 and 1024 context, then say where the memory actually goes and why that drove FlashAttention.
answer_points: Q, K, V are [B,H,S,d_h]; the scores are [B,H,S,S]; the output returns to [B,H,S,d_h] before W_O concatenates the heads
The score matrix is S/d_h times larger than its inputs — 16× at S=1024 with d_h=64, and 64× at S=4096
A naive implementation materialises that matrix twice, after QKᵀ and after the softmax, and that is precisely the traffic FlashAttention's tiling removes

In cross-attention Q comes from a different sequence than K and V, so the matrix is [S_q, S_kv] — assuming it is square is the bug that surfaces the first time you implement prefix caching or an encoder-decoder

concept: Splitting d_model into H heads of width d_model/H costs nothing in parameters or FLOPs but changes what the layer can express. A single head computes one attention distribution, so it can only attend to one thing per position. H heads compute H independent distributions in disjoint subspaces. The output projection then mixes those subspaces back together — without W_O the heads would never interact, and concatenation alone would leave them permanently independent.
example: GPT-2 small: d_model=768, H=12, d_h=64. Collapsing to H=1 with d_h=768 leaves the parameter count identical at 4·768² = 2.36M per layer and the FLOPs unchanged, but the layer can now form one attention pattern per position instead of twelve. Heads demonstrably specialise — previous-token heads, matching-bracket heads, syntactic heads — and a substantial fraction can be pruned at inference, though not the specialised ones.
interview_question: Parameters and FLOPs are identical whether you use 1 head of width 768 or 12 heads of width 64. So what does head count actually buy you, and how would you pick it?
answer_points: H independent softmax distributions rather than one, so the layer can attend to several distinct things at each position simultaneously
Each head works in a d_model/H subspace, so raising H buys diversity at the cost of per-head width
W_O is not optional — it mixes the concatenated subspaces, and without it the heads never communicate at all

Pushing d_h too low hurts: below roughly 64 the per-head rank is too small for an expressive score matrix, which is why models scale H with d_model and hold d_h fixed at 64 or 128 rather than fixing H

formula: \begin{gathered} dV = P^{\top}dO, \qquad dP = dO\,V^{\top} \\[3pt] dS = P \odot \big(dP - \mathrm{rowsum}(dP \odot P)\big) \\[3pt] dQ = \frac{dS\,K}{\sqrt{d_k}}, \qquad dK = \frac{dS^{\top}Q}{\sqrt{d_k}} \end{gathered}
concept: Gradients reach Q, K and V by three different routes. The V path is linear: out = PV, so dV = PᵀdO and dP = dO Vᵀ. The Q and K paths both pass through the softmax Jacobian, diag(p) − ppᵀ per row, which collapses to dS = P ⊙ (dP − rowsum(dP ⊙ P)). Attention trains well largely because that V path never crosses a saturating nonlinearity — the only saturation risk is the softmax itself, which is exactly what the 1/√d_k scaling exists to control.
example: The backward pass needs P, the [B,H,S,S] probability matrix. At B=4, H=12, S=1024 that is 50M elements, 100 MB in fp16 — and a naive implementation also keeps the pre-softmax scores, doubling it to 200 MB per layer, or 2.4 GB across 12 layers for attention alone. FlashAttention instead saves only the per-row max and log-sum-exp: 4·12·1024 rows × 2 floats × 4 bytes = 393 KB, a 500× reduction, and recomputes P from those.
interview_question: Trace the gradient from the attention output back to Q, then explain why FlashAttention's backward pass is faster even though it recomputes the entire score matrix.
answer_points: Three routes: dV = PᵀdO is linear and clean, dP = dO Vᵀ, then through the softmax dS = P ⊙ (dP − rowsum(dP ⊙ P)), and finally dQ = dS·K/√d_k
That rowsum term is the off-diagonal part of the softmax Jacobian diag(p) − ppᵀ, and dropping it is the most common error in a hand derivation
Storing P for the backward costs B·H·S² and dominates activation memory; FlashAttention keeps only the row max and log-sum-exp, two floats per row
Recomputation wins because attention is memory-bound — rebuilding P in SRAM burns FLOPs that were idle anyway, while the HBM traffic saved is the real bottleneck
Dropout sits after the softmax, so its mask must be saved or regenerated from the same seed, or the backward silently disagrees with the forward
